strengths: The construction provides an understandable connection between discriminative partitions and class-conditional Gaussian mixtures. Reusing forest leaves or ReLU activation regions is of interest to researchers studying density estimation and predictive uncertainty.

The five synthetic problems provide useful visualizations of posterior extrapolation. Figure 2 reports 45 repetitions with interquartile bands, and Table 1 shows substantial OOD-detection improvements over the parent models in the evaluated settings.
The motivation and main pipeline are accessible, and the manuscript supplies pseudocode and a code link. A focused study of these low-dimensional phenomena has an identifiable research audience.
weaknesses: Necessary: Theorem 1's proof contains substantive errors. A shrinking Gaussian does not become uniform over its polytope, so the argument following Eq. (4.2) does not establish the asserted kernel limit. Counts in partitions learned from the same observations are not automatically binomial, and neither the covariance sum nor contributions from an increasing number of neighboring kernels are controlled. Furthermore, asymptotic unbiasedness alone would establish neither density consistency nor the abstract's claimed efficiency advantage over discriminative models. Supply a valid result with applicable assumptions, or remove the unsupported theoretical claims.

Necessary: The performance conclusions contradict Figure 2. At small sample sizes on Gaussian XOR, KDF and KDN have substantially worse Hellinger distances than their respective parents; on Circle, KDF also has higher classification error over a substantial sample-size range. These results contradict the statements that posterior estimates are always closer and that OOD detection comes without any in-distribution sacrifice. The abstract's account of the sample-size trade-off also needs reconciliation with the plots.

Necessary: Narrow the OOD claims to what is established. Equation (3.8) approaches the empirical class prior far from the data, which is uniform only for balanced priors. This does not guarantee the desired behavior throughout the support complement in Eq. (2.1), including regions near the support. Evaluation outside the training square supports a limited extrapolation result, not general OOD robustness. Also distinguish the proper Gaussian-mixture density from the nonnormalizable score obtained by adding a positive constant over all of R^d.

Necessary: Resolve the inconsistent KDN definition. Equation (3.4) measures differences between preactivations, whereas Algorithm 3 accumulates differences between postactivations. These produce different weights; with one hidden layer, the preactivation expression is identically zero because the first-layer preactivation is globally affine. Specify which construction generated the experiments and make the equations and algorithms agree.

Necessary: Important experimental and implementation details are missing. Report the values and selection procedures for h, T, and C; covariance regularization for sparsely populated polytopes; training termination; and the training/test sampling protocol. Define the OOD detection score and the uncertainty summaries in Table 1. Its caption calls FPR@95 a false-negative rate, while the text calls it a false-positive rate. The Gaussian XOR description also assigns identical Gaussian mixtures to both classes, inconsistent with the plotted task. These omissions and contradictions impede reproduction and interpretation.

Necessary: The human experiment does not establish the claimed similarity in individual uncertainty. Figure 3 averages class probabilities and does not include KDF or KDN. A population mean near 0.5 can arise from opposing confident responses, so it does not demonstrate that individual participants are uncertain. Analyze individual confidence and directly compare the proposed models with human responses on matched trials, or restrict the conclusion to the observed aggregate pattern.

Optional: A conventional class-conditional KDE or Gaussian-mixture baseline using the same additive bias, together with an ablation of that bias, would help isolate the contribution of learned partitions. Larger Figure 2 panels and removal of the empty Appendix Algorithm 5 would improve presentation. These improvements are secondary to the correctness and evidential gaps above.
